content: 1. The WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) for syphilis treatment included experts from various regions and institutions worldwide. These experts were tasked with reviewing and updating the guidelines for the treatment of Treponema pallidum (syphilis). 2. The GDG reviewed existing international guidelines, including those from the CDC (2010), the British Association for Sexual Health and HIV (2006–2011), the Public Health Agency of Canada (2013–2014), the International Union of Sexually Transmitted Infections (IUSTI), and others. This review aimed to identify areas requiring updates or new recommendations. 3. Four categories of sexually transmitted infection (STI) conditions were prioritized for review: Conditions included in the 2003 WHO STI guidelines that were selected for review and update. Conditions not included in the 2003 guidelines but deemed important and common enough to be added. Rare conditions included in the 2003 guidelines that were not updated but retained in the new guidelines. Conditions not included in the 2003 guidelines and not selected for inclusion in the new guidelines. 4. Surveys were conducted among GDG members to rank the importance of populations, interventions, and outcomes for specific STI conditions. These rankings were based on a scale of 1 to 9, with higher scores indicating greater priority. Outcomes with average scores of 7–9 were considered critical, 4–6 were important, and 1–3 were not important. 5. For congenital syphilis, treatment options were evaluated for various scenarios: Scenario 1: Infants with confirmed congenital syphilis were recommended to receive benzyl penicillin (100,000–150,000 U/kg/day for 10–15 days) or procaine penicillin (50,000 U/kg/day for 10–15 days). Ceftriaxone was also an option, with dosing adjusted for infants under or over 30 days of age. Scenario 2: Infants clinically normal but born to mothers with untreated, inadequately treated, or non-penicillin-treated syphilis were recommended similar regimens, including benzyl penicillin, procaine penicillin, or ceftriaxone. Scenario 3: Infants clinically normal and born to mothers adequately treated for syphilis with no signs of reinfection were recommended a single dose of benzathine penicillin (50,000 U/kg intramuscularly) or no treatment, depending on clinical judgment. 6. The GDG used a hierarchical approach to evidence synthesis, prioritizing pre-existing systematic reviews and conducting new reviews when necessary. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included for critical and important outcomes, while non-randomized studies were considered when RCT evidence was unavailable. 7. Data extraction and analysis were conducted systematically. Two researchers independently screened studies, resolved disagreements through discussion, and extracted data on patient characteristics, interventions, and outcomes. Statistical analyses included pooling results from RCTs and non-randomized studies using random-effects models, with heterogeneity explored when I² exceeded 50%. 8. The GDG framed nine key questions for updating the syphilis guidelines using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) format. These questions addressed treatment regimens for early and late syphilis, including considerations for pregnant women, individuals with penicillin allergies, and infants with congenital syphilis. 9. The guideline development process emphasized critical outcomes such as clinical cure, serologic response, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, and neonatal health outcomes (e.g., low birth weight, stillbirth, congenital deformities). Important outcomes included antimicrobial resistance, STI complications, partner transmission, and side effects. 10. The GDG ensured that the recommendations were evidence-based, feasible, and equitable, considering patient values, acceptability, and cost-effectiveness. The process involved extensive consultation, systematic reviews, and iterative feedback to refine the guidelines.
